title: Christmas is a season
hookLine: the octave and the season run on to the Baptism of the Lord

cards: December twenty-sixth. The wrapping paper's in the recycling. The radio has abruptly stopped playing carols.
By New Year's, trees lie on the curb, needles everywhere. For most of the culture, Christmas is one day, and the day after, it's over.

But walk into a Catholic church on December twenty-sixth, or on January fifth, and the tree is still lit, the crib is still there, the priest is still in white, and people are still singing Christmas hymns.
The party hasn't ended. It's barely started.

teach.b: In the Church's calendar, Christmas is a season, not a day. It begins on Christmas Eve and runs until the feast of the Baptism of the Lord, in early to mid January. Inside it are three layers.

teach.h: THE OCTAVE: EIGHT DAYS AS ONE.
teach.b: The Church gives Christmas and Easter an octave: the celebration lasts eight days, as if it's all one long day of joy.
The Christmas octave runs from December twenty-fifth to January first, which Catholics keep as the Solemnity of Mary, the Mother of God.
Second, the twelve days, the old count from Christmas to the Epiphany on January sixth, the one in the song.

teach.h: ON TO THE BAPTISM OF THE LORD.
teach.b: Third, the full season, running on to the Baptism of the Lord, when the adult Jesus stands in the Jordan; the next day, Ordinary Time begins.

Following an old custom, some families keep their crib up even longer, until Candlemas on February second. The word itself is simple: Christmas is Christ's Mass, from old English, named after the Mass. Why so long?
After the shepherds came and went, the Douay-Rheims says: "But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." She didn't move on. She kept turning it over, and the Church asks the same.
The feast is too big for one day, so the days after it are full of feasts: Stephen, whom tradition calls the first martyr, John the apostle, the Holy Innocents, the Holy Family.
The whole season is a slow pondering of one astonishing claim: God was born.

how: Catholics keep Christmas as a season: churches stay decorated and white vestments are worn through the octave and the twelve days until the Baptism of the Lord, and some families leave the tree and crib up until then.

games.q: you're Mary. the shepherds have come and gone, full of news about angels. what do you do?
o: keep it all, pondering it in your heart.
put it behind you and get back to normal.
games.why: "But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." the long season asks the same: keep turning it over.

practice: Think of one thing from Christmas, this past one or the next, that you could keep going a little longer: a light in the window, a song, a habit of calling someone, a crib on a shelf.
Picture it still there in the middle of January, still celebrating when everyone else has stopped. If you pray, ponder one line of the Christmas story, the way Mary did.

wordCard.voice: Octave. Eight days kept as one long day of joy, the Christmas octave running from December twenty-fifth to January first. Today's word.

orig.note: Old English: Christ's Mass, the source of the word Christmas.

carryVoice: Your line: Christmas isn't one day. An octave, twelve days, a whole season. That's day one hundred forty-five.
